text:
*Interview with Félix Monnier, nephew of the deceased, in the dining room.*

MATTHEY: Monsieur Monnier, I am sorry to keep you up. Please sit down. You are Aurèle Monnier's nephew?

FÉLIX: His brother's son. Jules's boy. My father died in 1889, and since then my uncle has been the only family I have. Please don't look at me like that, Inspector, or I shall start laughing and then you will think me a monster.

MATTHEY: Tell me about the evening, from dinner.

FÉLIX: We sat down as usual. When the temple bell struck nine, I looked at my watch, and it said twenty minutes to nine. My uncle makes everyone show their watches every year, and he made a scene about mine in front of everyone. He said it was a disgrace to my father's memory. Coming from a man who could never leave a movement alone, that was rich.

MATTHEY: What did he say about your watch?

FÉLIX: That it had not gone properly since my father died, and that I should take it to a jeweller to be melted down. I said I would sooner give him my debts. That was not a good joke, and I knew it as I said it.

MATTHEY: Where did you go after dinner?

FÉLIX: Up to the library. I stayed there alone. I had a brandy, by myself, and I was not drunk, whatever anyone tells you.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything from the library?

FÉLIX: At eighteen minutes past ten by my watch I heard a thump on the floor right above me, in the atelier. Then my uncle's repeater sounding. I know that sound. Ten slow deep notes, and I counted those. Then some doubled notes, then quick high ones. I did not count those. By then I was not counting anything.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anyone on the stairs?

FÉLIX: At a quarter past ten by my watch someone went quickly up the stairs, past the library door. I heard that. At twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch someone came quickly down. I did not see who it was. The door was shut, so I saw nothing at all.

MATTHEY: Did you leave the library before anyone came to it?

FÉLIX: No. I stayed there alone until Bastien Girard came in, at thirty-two minutes past ten by my watch. We sat together there until the temple struck eleven. He wanted to talk about the repeater, and what it would fetch, I think, though he did not say so in those words.

MATTHEY: Had you and Monsieur Girard any business between you?

FÉLIX: I owe him some money. Not a great deal, but enough that he is never friendly about it. He and my uncle quarrelled over the price of the repeater at dinner, you may have heard them. Girard is a blunt man. He is not a thief, if that is what you are asking.

MATTHEY: I am asking what you know, Monsieur. You say you carry a watch of your father's?

FÉLIX: A silver one. It has run badly since he died, and I have never let anyone touch it. Not a jeweller, and not my uncle, who laughed at it at dinner. It is the only thing of his I have, Inspector. I am not going to hand it over to be tidied.

MATTHEY: And the repeater? What did it mean to your uncle?

FÉLIX: Everything. He was building it for the new century, and he said so every day. He spoke of it the way other men speak of their sons. I think it frightened him that it might be finished without him, though he would never have admitted that.

MATTHEY: Thank you. Is there anything you wish to add?

FÉLIX: Only that I was alone on the floor below the atelier, Inspector, and I know how that looks. I have been turning it over since I sat down, and it does not look well for me at all.

MATTHEY: I have not said how anything looks, Monsieur.
